owned_question: When a system records, compares, or schedules events and dependencies, which ordering claims are licensed by the evidence (causal order, clock order, observation order) versus merely imposed by representation — and what does a cycle check or topological schedule actually prove about the world?
non_collapse_laws: a topological rank is scheduling advice over one observed snapshot, not causal proof about future editions of the graph
absence of detected cycles differs from proof of acyclicity under incomplete observation
a happens-before relation is not implication: A before B licenses neither 'A caused B' nor 'A could have prevented B'
clock equality does not mean simultaneity; Lamport-clock comparability is established only along message edges, never between unrelated processes
flattening a partial order into a total order is a commitment to arbitrariness that must be marked as tie-broken, not derived
replay in recorded order preserves causality only if every effect was idempotent at its original position in the order
carrier_requirements: an explicit event record with identity, source process, and logical timestamp(s)
an edge store for dependency/lineage graphs carrying edition or epoch stamps so cycle tests can be invalidated when edges change
declared knowledge bounds: which processes/events an observer has actually seen (needed to distinguish 'no cycle found' from 'acyclic')
an idempotency key contract per replayable effect so ordering rules can distinguish safe re-execution from double-application
invariants: if annotate_happens_before(a,b) then compare_order(a,b) <= 0 in every totalization that respects the partial order
detect_cycle must be a pure function of a stated edge-set edition; changing editions voids prior verdicts
schedule_topo output on a DAG with no ties may vary, but must never invert any asserted precedence edge
merge_clocks monotonicity: receiving a clock message never lowers the receiver's clock
provenance event chains satisfy generation-precedes-usage; validity fails iff the precedes graph contains a strict-precedes cycle
every topological rank emitted carries the observation scope (which edges were visible) alongside the ranking
refusals: refuse to certify 'B was caused by A' from temporal precedence alone
refuse to declare a graph acyclic when the edge store is known incomplete or stale
refuse to compare logical clocks across disconnected components without a shared synchronization event
refuse a topological schedule when cycle detection returns positive; emit the offending cycle instead of a best-effort ordering
refuse replay guarantees for effects lacking an idempotency key, regardless of correct ordering
counterexamples: Lamport-clock equality across unrelated processes mistaken for simultaneity: C(a)=C(b) proves nothing without a message chain
DFS-based cycle test invalidated by stale edge editions: graph declared acyclic at epoch n, a later edition adds the back-edge, cached verdict silently wrong
lineage topology mistaken for business impact: a node deep in the DAG dominates by blast radius even though its topological rank is lowest-dependency
total-order flattening hides concurrency: two concurrent events serialized by arbitrary tiebreak are later read as if the system asserted their real sequence
authority_limit: This axis adjudicates orderings and graph-structural claims derivable from recorded events and declared dependencies. It cannot certify physical causation, real-time simultaneity, future acyclicity, or business importance of lineage nodes; those require carriers outside this axis.
